claim: - [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — approved the OSAID through its 10-person board rather than a full membership vote
- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — holds that a machine-learning application is not free unless its [[TrainingData]] and processing scripts respect the four freedoms
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — defends omitting full training data so that [[OpenSourceAI]] can exist in fields like medical AI where data cannot be legally shared
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — announced that DeepSeek-R1's code and models are released under the MIT License, permitting free distillation and commercialization
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — describes DeepSeek-R1 as a "fully open-source model" accompanied by a technical report
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — announced a license update making DeepSeek-R1 MIT licensed so the community can leverage its model weights and outputs
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — announced that DeepSeek-R1 API outputs can now be used for fine-tuning and distillation
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — released 6 small models distilled from DeepSeek-R1 as fully open-sourced models
- [analysis] [[DeepSeek]] — claims DeepSeek-R1 performs on par with OpenAI-o1 on math, code, and reasoning tasks
- [analysis] [[DeepSeek]] — claims its distilled 32B and 70B models perform on par with OpenAI-o1-mini
- [analysis] [[DeepSeek]] — attributes R1's performance boost to large-scale reinforcement learning in post-training that needed minimal labeled data
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — prices DeepSeek-R1 API access at $0.14 per million input tokens on a cache hit, $0.55 per million input tokens on a cache miss, and $2.19 per million output tokens
- [fact] [[DeepSeek]] — made DeepSeek-R1 available on its website and through its API under the model name `deepseek-reasoner`
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — announced on 2024-10-22 that it is preparing a statement of criteria to determine when a machine-learning application is free
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — stated that the criteria are being drafted by a working group of FSF board members, staff, and management that consulted external experts
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — stated that serious work toward a unanimous conclusion began in May 2024 and has concluded, with the working group now drafting the exact definition text
- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — describes machine-learning applications as only partially software, since each also includes model parameters produced by training

- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — argues that training data is not the "source code" of model parameters in the usual sense, because parameters are not a translation of anything a human author wrote

- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — explains that in practice users study and adapt a machine-learning application by running it over different prompt data, analyzing its training data, and retraining it, rather than by editing parameters directly

- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — stated that all software in a free machine-learning application must grant every user the four freedoms, covering both the training software and the inference software
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — stated that it cannot call a machine-learning application free unless all of its [[TrainingData]] and the related processing scripts respect the four freedoms

- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — holds that granting the four freedoms may require the release to include the model parameters, with users permitted to use and redistribute the parameters and modified versions of them
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — stated that machine-learning applications that do not offer the four freedoms to all users are nonfree even if their software components are free

- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — allows that some nonfree machine-learning applications may have valid moral reasons for withholding training data, citing personal medical data as the example
- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — holds that using such a nonfree application could be ethically excusable if it does a job vital to society, such as diagnosing disease or injury

- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — set two conditions for considering that use just: the component software must be free, and the application must be distributed in a form that supports incremental training or retraining from scratch
- [fact] [[Meta]] — released Llama 2 free of charge for research and commercial use, calling the release open source
- [fact] [[Meta]] — included model weights and starting code for both the pretrained model and the conversational fine-tuned versions
- [fact] [[Meta]] — reported more than 100,000 requests from researchers for access to Llama 1
- [fact] [[Meta]] — named Microsoft its preferred partner for Llama 2, a partnership Satya Nadella announced on stage at Microsoft Inspire
- [fact] [[Meta]] — made Llama 2 available in the Azure AI model catalog starting on the announcement day
- [fact] [[Meta]] — optimized Llama 2 to run locally on Windows
- [fact] [[Meta]] — made Llama 2 available through Amazon Web Services, Hugging Face, and other providers
- [analysis] [[Meta]] — argues an open approach is right for generative AI because it gives businesses, startups, and researchers tools and computing power they could not build themselves
- [analysis] [[Meta]] — argues opening access to AI models is safer, because developers and researchers can stress test them and fix problems as a community
- [fact] [[Meta]] — red-teamed its fine-tuned models through internal efforts and commissioned third parties to run external adversarial testing
- [forecast] [[Meta]] — plans to release updated fine-tuned models based on continued safety fine-tuning and benchmarking
- [fact] [[Meta]] — disclosed known challenges and mitigations in a transparency schematic inside the Llama 2 research paper
- [fact] [[Meta]] — published a Responsible Use Guide of best practices for responsible development and safety evaluation
- [fact] [[Meta]] — put in place an Acceptable Use Policy that prohibits certain use cases of Llama 2
- [fact] [[Meta]] — launched the Open Innovation AI Research Community, a partnership program for academic researchers
- [fact] [[Meta]] — announced the Llama Impact Challenge for public, non-profit, and for-profit entities to apply Llama 2 to environmental, education, and other challenges
- [analysis] [[Meta]] — cites React and PyTorch, frameworks its engineers developed and shared, as open-source precedents that became industry standards
- [fact] [[Meta]] — defines the licensed "Llama 3.1" materials to include trained model weights plus inference-enabling, training-enabling, and fine-tuning-enabling code
- [fact] [[Meta]] — grants a non-exclusive, worldwide, non-transferable, royalty-free limited license to use, reproduce, distribute, copy, modify, and create derivative works of the Llama materials
- [fact] [[Meta]] — requires anyone who distributes the Llama materials or a product containing them to provide a copy of the agreement
- [fact] [[Meta]] — requires distributors to prominently display "Built with Llama" on a related website, user interface, blog post, about page, or product documentation
- [fact] [[Meta]] — requires anyone who uses Llama materials or outputs to create, train, or fine-tune a distributed AI model to put "Llama" at the beginning of that model's name
- [fact] [[Meta]] — requires every distributed copy to carry a "Notice" text file stating that Llama 3.1 is licensed under the Llama 3.1 Community License
- [fact] [[Meta]] — requires all use of the Llama materials to follow a separate Acceptable Use Policy, which the agreement incorporates by reference

- [fact] [[Meta]] — withholds the license from any licensee whose products had more than 700 million monthly active users in the calendar month before the release date, until Meta grants a license at its sole discretion
- [fact] [[Meta]] — provides the Llama materials and their outputs "as is," disclaiming all warranties, including non-infringement and fitness for a particular purpose
- [fact] [[Meta]] — grants no trademark license beyond using the "Llama" mark to meet the naming requirement
- [fact] [[Meta]] — assigns licensees ownership of the derivative works and modifications they make, subject to Meta's ownership of the Llama materials
- [fact] [[Meta]] — terminates a licensee's rights on the date that licensee files an intellectual-property claim against Meta over the Llama materials or their outputs
- [fact] [[Meta]] — may terminate the agreement on any breach, after which the licensee must delete and stop using the Llama materials
- [fact] [[Meta]] — makes California law govern the agreement and gives California courts exclusive jurisdiction over disputes
- [fact] [[MistralAI]] — announced the Mistral AI Non-Production License (MNPL) in a blog post dated May 29, 2024
- [fact] [[MistralAI]] — states that the MNPL allows developers to use its technology for non-commercial purposes and to support research work [[mistral-ai-non-production-license#Key Quotes|self]]
- [fact] [[MistralAI]] — released Codestral under the MNPL on the day of the announcement

- [fact] [[MistralAI]] — says it will keep releasing models and code under Apache 2.0 while it consolidates two product families, one under Apache 2.0 and one under the MNPL [[mistral-ai-non-production-license#Key Quotes|self]]
- [analysis] [[MistralAI]] — explains that community members and partners building high-margin products on its models sometimes fail to contribute to its success, research, and independence
- [analysis] [[MistralAI]] — says the MNPL is meant to ensure that businesses built on its work operate in a way that is fair and sustainable for all parties
- [analysis] [[MistralAI]] — describes the new license as striking a balance between its commitment to openness principles and its responsibility to grow its business
- [analysis] [[MistralAI]] — argues that openness in AI drives innovation and safeguards transparency and accountability
- [analysis] [[MistralAI]] — asserts that the debate over openness in AI is being used to entrench incumbent players in a competitive industry
- [forecast] [[MistralAI]] — pledges to keep defending openness in AI and to pursue its mission of putting frontier AI in the hands of everyone
- [fact] [[Mozilla]] — endorses the [[OpenSourceInitiative]]'s Open Source AI Definition as "an important step forward"
- [analysis] [[Mozilla]] — argues a binary definition gives developers, advocates, and regulators needed precision and helps fight [[OpenWashing]]
- [analysis] [[Mozilla]] — characterizes "open-ish models like Meta's Llama 3" as the kind of release the definition is meant to clarify
- [forecast] [[Mozilla]] — intends to make open datasets a more commonplace part of the AI ecosystem and will publish supporting norms
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — released version 1.0 of the Open Source AI Definition in the week before 2024-11-01
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — adopted the OECD definitions of an AI system and of machine learning for the OSAID
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires that source code used to train and run the system be available under OSI-approved licenses
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires sufficiently detailed information about the data used to train the system
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires that model parameters, including weights, be made available
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — decided that training data need not be available under an open license for a system to count as open source
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues that an open-data requirement would limit the OSAID's reach, since many datasets cannot be shared, for example for privacy reasons
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — opted for a binary, non-tiered standard, arguing it must be clear which systems comply
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — released the OSAID in October 2024, requiring data information, code, and parameters as the preferred form for modification
- [analysis] [[DeepSeek]] — R1 (January 2025, MIT-licensed weights) is an open-weights release because the weights are public but the [[TrainingData]] is not
- [fact] [[Meta]] — released Llama 3.1 405B, which it calls the first frontier-level open source AI model, along with new Llama 3.1 70B and 8B models
- [fact] [[Anthropic]] — states in the Opus 5 system card that the model can search for vulnerabilities in uncompiled source code but not in compiled software
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — published the first version of the OSAID on 2024-10-28
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — defines an [[OpenSourceAI]] system as one made available under terms that grant the freedom to use, study, modify, and share it
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires the "complete source code used to train and run the system" but not the [[TrainingData]] itself
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires data information that must list all publicly available training data and all third-party training data, and where to obtain each
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that the license for the Llama LLM is not an Open Source license, despite Meta describing LLaMa 2 as "open source"
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says it has asked [[Meta]] to correct its misstatement that LLaMa 2 is open source
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — welcomes Meta lowering barriers to access to powerful AI systems while rejecting the open-source label
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues Meta is confusing "open source" with "resources available to some users under some conditions"
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — questions whether the term "open source" can validly apply to a large language model made of several kinds of resources at all
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that under OSD points 5 and 6, an Open Source license may not discriminate against persons, groups, or fields of endeavor
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues paragraph 2 of the Llama Community License Agreement breaks the OSD by restricting commercial use for some users
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues the Llama Acceptable Use Policy breaks the OSD by restricting use of the model and software for certain purposes
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says it does not question Meta's wish to limit competitive use of Llama, but holds that doing so removes the license from the Open Source category
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues an Open Source license gives developers and users sovereignty to decide how and where to use a technology without engaging another party

- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — explains that the OSD bars field-of-use restrictions because future uses cannot be known beforehand, citing the Linux kernel's spread into medical devices, airplanes, and rockets
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues Meta's policy prohibits use in potentially beneficial areas such as regulated or controlled substances and critical infrastructure
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues that even a clause requiring users to follow the law is problematic when laws differ between places or are unjust
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states it is running a series of events to craft a common definition of "open" in the AI context and is inviting submissions of ideas

- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that Llama 3.x, released under new licensing terms since its call on Meta a year earlier, still fails the Open Source Definition [[osi-meta-llama-2-license-not-open-source#Key Claims|OSI's 2023 Llama 2 post]]
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says Meta keeps falsely promoting Llama as "Open Source"
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — calls on the community to ask Mark Zuckerberg and Yann LeCun to change the Llama license to comply with the Open Source Definition
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — holds that the new Open Source AI Definition v1.0 is not needed to judge whether the Llama 3.x community licenses convey basic freedoms
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — agrees with the Free Software Foundation's recent evaluation that the Llama 3.1 Community License fails freedom 0, the freedom to use the model for any purpose
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that the Llama 3.1 Community License fails OSD point 5 by discriminating against users
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that the Llama 3.1 Community License fails OSD point 6 by restricting fields of endeavour
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says these restrictions were already present in the Llama 2 license and all remain in the newer licenses
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that newer versions of the Llama community license exclude any persons in the European Union from using the model, without explanation
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues the OSAID created no confusion about Llama's proprietary nature, since Meta's open washing and the OSI's response to it predate the OSAID

- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says unnamed individuals who tie their criticism of the OSAID to Meta's use of the term are supporting Meta's open washing and sowing fear, uncertainty, and doubt
- [forecast] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says it will keep fighting open washing through public statements, events, and education aimed at the Open Source and AI communities, lawmakers, and businesses
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — defines an [[OpenSourceAI]] system by four freedoms (use, study, modify, share) plus required access to data information, code, and parameters
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — validated Pythia, OLMo, Amber, CrystalCoder, and T5 as OSAID-compliant, and judged [[Meta]]'s Llama 2 non-compliant
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues a binary definition is needed to inform regulators and to combat [[OpenWashing]]
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — treats [[OpenWeights]] models as a separate category that does not satisfy the full freedoms
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that the four software freedoms are the freedoms to use, study, modify, and share without asking permission from the rights holder
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — puts the demand-side value of the Open Source ecosystem at $8.8 trillion
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — describes an AI model as three main components: training data, weights/parameters, and code for data preparation and training
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — holds that a user's access to those components determines whether an AI system is closed, open-weight, or Open Source
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says [[OpenWeights]] models let users run the model locally, paying only for electricity and hardware, or host it through a third-party provider
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — says open weights let users [[FineTuning|fine-tune]] a model on their own data, keeping control of that data
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — names ChatGPT, Claude, and many autonomous driving systems as examples of fully closed models
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues that open-weight models limit the freedom to modify a model and prevent users from fully studying it
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — argues that without the code and [[TrainingData]], a user cannot fully inspect why a model gives an output or whether that output can be trusted

- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — states that [[OpenSourceAI]] under its definition releases the weights, the training code, and either the training data or a detailed account of how the data was built

- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — reports that researchers used Ai2's Olmo, with its full training dataset and model checkpoints, to inject new information into training data and observe how the model memorized or forgot it

- [forecast] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — expects the next phase of AI development to depend on recognizing that Open Source AI is "where the real innovation lies"
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — scheduled its board vote on the Open Source AI Definition for 2024-10-27, with version 1.0 slated for publication on 2024-10-28

- [fact] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — announced in June 2023, as OSI executive director, the organization's intent to define open-source AI, objecting to models "claiming to be 'open' or 'Open Source'" while adding restrictions that break the Open Source Definition
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — held the definition's kickoff meeting on 2023-06-21 at [[Mozilla]]'s San Francisco headquarters, then ran in-person and online sessions plus an online forum
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — takes the draft's definition of an AI system from the OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires in the draft the source code for training and running the system, the model parameters, and "sufficiently detailed information" about the training data
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires data information and model parameters to be available under "OSI-approved terms" rather than OSI-approved licenses
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — does not require release of the [[TrainingData]] itself, only detailed information about it
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — published draft version 0.0.9 on 2024-08-22, acknowledging training data as "one of the most hotly debated parts of the definition"
- [analysis] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — concluded that training data is a benefit rather than a requirement because it is not part of the preferred form for modifying an existing AI system
- [fact] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — announced it is working on a statement of criteria for free machine-learning applications
- [analysis] [[FreeSoftwareFoundation]] — holds that an ML application is not free unless all its training data and processing scripts respect the four freedoms

- [analysis] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — rejects the claim that the OSAID lowers the bar, saying neither the more-components camp nor the weights-and-architecture camp offers an optimal approach
- [analysis] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — attributes the OSAID's preferred form for modification to its list of endorsers and to Carnegie Mellon University's comment, not to himself or the OSI board
- [analysis] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — says a "simple translation" of the Open Source Definition to AI would not work

- [fact] [[Meta]] — introduced Llama 3 as "the next generation of our state-of-the-art open source large language model" [[rethinking-open-source-generative-ai#Key Quotes]]
- [fact] [[Meta]] — declined to comment on the letter
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — released version 1.0 of the Open Source AI Definition on 2024-10-28 after several years of collaboration with academia and industry
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires an open source AI model to provide enough information about its design that a person could "substantially" recreate it
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — requires disclosure of training-data provenance, processing, and how the data can be obtained or licensed
- [fact] [[OpenSourceInitiative]] — grants users the freedom to use the model for any purpose and to modify it without asking permission

- [fact] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — said OSI did explicit outreach to diverse stakeholders, including organizations that most often talk to regulators
- [fact] [[StefanoMaffulli]] — said Google and Microsoft agreed to drop the term "open source" for models that are not fully open after discussions with OSI, but Meta has not

- [fact] [[Meta]] — said it is taking a "cautious approach" to sharing model details, including training data, as regulations such as California's training transparency law evolve

- [fact] [[HuggingFace]] — describes GPT OSS as an open-weights release by OpenAI designed for reasoning, agentic tasks, and developer use cases

- [fact] [[HuggingFace]] — states that the 20B model runs within 16 GB of memory, including consumer GPUs such as the 3090, 4090, and 5080

- [fact] [[Anthropic]] — reports that the campaigns found techniques that tricked the model into revealing its thinking traces directly

- [fact] [[Anthropic]] — reports that nearly 300,000 requests reached Claude over one 10-day period through a network of 5,000 accounts, mainly targeting its Opus model

- [analysis] [[EleutherAI]] — claims the Comma models rival [[Meta]]'s first Llama model on benchmarks for coding, image understanding and math
- [forecast] [[EleutherAI]] — commits to releasing open datasets more frequently with its research and infrastructure partners
